title: Keep calm and regulate on: Inside the EU's response to AI extinction warnings
content:
An Anthropic employee quit with a stark warning that the artificial intelligence models being built "could kill us all by the end of the decade." | Riccardo Milani/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — A viral social media post warning that top American AI developers are "gambling with our lives" has been met this week in Brussels with business as usual — and a splash of Schadenfreude.
The European Union's corridors of power were one of the few places over the past 48 hours not overtaken by a frenzy after an Anthropic employee announced he was quitting, with a stark warning that the people building AI "earnestly believe" that the artificial intelligence models they're building "could kill us all by the end of the decade."
Multiple EU policymakers responded to questions about such a threat by noting that Brussels already has a law for that: the bloc's Artificial Intelligence Act.
Advertisement
Others noted that the dire AI extinction warning could actually be a chance for the bloc's highest officials to regain control over the AI narrative. Since the groundbreaking 2022 release of ChatGPT, the EU was repeatedly mocked by tech enthusiasts for regulating a still-emerging technology.
European officials say they can now claim they'd understood the risks that others are only now waking up to. "In my view, the EU has already legislated for exactly this scenario: it is called the AI Act," said Michael McNamara, an Irish European Parliament lawmaker, who's the co-lead of the Parliament's group monitoring AI.
A leading European AI CEO, Uljan Sharka of Italy-based Domyn, which develops models for regulated industries, called Tuesday's post on X by Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher: "ridiculous." Sharka argued that the panic set off presents a "massive opportunity" for European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at her State of the European Union speech next week to "explain why the AI Act exists."
Michael McNamara, an Irish European Parliament lawmaker, who's the co-lead of the Parliament's group monitoring AI. | Gianluigi Guercia/AFP via Getty Images
The "keep calm" attitude has been the mantra among EU policymakers: don't get carried away by the hype or incidents; trust the law Europe has in place.
"The EU already has a legal framework to regulate and mitigate the risk posed by advanced models," said European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier in a statement shared with POLITICO.
Systemic risks
Under the bloc's AI law, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic must take into account and counter what are called "systemic risks." These include the risk of losing control of a model, or the risk that a model is no longer aligned with human goals and values (known as "misalignment").
Advertisement
The Commission's Artificial Intelligence Office enforces this monitoring, and has contracted leading independent AI researchers, such as those from METR, an independent non-profit research organization based in California, to carry out the regulatory oversight.
Indeed, it was METR that was called in by OpenAI researchers to investigate after a much-discussed July hack of AI company Hugging Face, when OpenAI-powered agents went rogue.
One sign that Brussels wants to focus on enforcing the current lawwas the confirmation Thursday that European Parliament lawmakers would raise the AI extinction warning for discussion on Sept. 30, as part of a regular enforcement check-in with the European Commission.
They urged the Commission to increase the pressure on the companies and to enforce the law.
"This is exactly why the AI Act created obligations for systemic-risk models. Europe must now enforce them fully," said Italian Social-Democrat Brando Benifei, the Parliament's other lead of the group in charge of monitoring AI.
Domyn's Sharka said that von der Leyen should use her State of the Union speech on Wednesday to lay out a vision for how Europe can compete in the AI development race without sacrificing its leadership in regulating the powerful technology.
"One of the points where Europe is failing is that it does things in the right way, but we're not explaining them enough," Sharka said. "This is not about slowing down innovation; this is about building actually even faster, but with a safe approach."

report.summary: EU officials respond to an Anthropic employee's AI extinction warning by pointing to the bloc's existing AI Act, urging calm and full enforcement.
report.background: The warning came from Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher, whose viral post claimed AI builders believe their models could kill us all by decade's end. Brussels was largely unmoved. Since ChatGPT's 2022 release, EU officials have been mocked for regulating an emerging technology, but they now argue the AI Act anticipated systemic risks. The law requires advanced-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic to assess and mitigate risks such as loss of control and misalignment. The European Commission's AI Office enforces these duties and has contracted independent researchers, including California-based METR. Lawmakers are set to discuss the warning on Sept. 30, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen faces pressure to explain the AI Act in her State of the European Union speech.
key_points: Brussels treated the AI extinction warning as business as usual, with policymakers saying the EU already has a law for such risks: the AI Act. Officials also saw a chance to reclaim the AI narrative after years of being mocked for regulating the technology early.

The AI Act imposes systemic-risk obligations on frontier model developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. They must consider and counter risks including loss of control over a model and misalignment with human goals and values, with enforcement handled by the Commission's AI Office.

The European Parliament's AI monitoring group will raise the extinction warning on Sept. 30 in a regular enforcement check-in. Lawmakers urged the Commission to increase pressure on companies and fully enforce the law's systemic-risk obligations.

Industry reaction was split. Italian AI CEO Uljan Sharka called the viral warning ridiculous, arguing the panic presents an opportunity for Ursula von der Leyen to explain why the AI Act exists and to frame safe AI development as faster, not slower.

The EU's response emphasizes enforcement over new emergency legislation. Brussels wants to show that its early regulatory bet was justified, while using independent experts like METR to support oversight of advanced AI systems.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the EU's stance signals regulatory continuity rather than a crisis-driven overhaul. Frontier labs face growing pressure to document systemic-risk assessments, run third-party evaluations, and demonstrate alignment and control measures, especially if Brussels tightens enforcement. Developers should expect compliance work around model transparency, incident reporting, and independent audits to become more operational. For regular users, the immediate effect is limited, but the debate strengthens expectations that powerful AI systems will face public accountability and safety checks. Globally, the EU hopes its calm response makes the AI Act a reference point for governing existential-risk claims without halting innovation.
report.tools: Readers can follow METR's independent evaluations of frontier models, the EU AI Office's guidance and enforcement notices, and the European Parliament's AI monitoring group. For hands-on safety testing, open-source projects such as HELM, Inspect, and Garak offer evaluation and red-teaming frameworks. Hugging Face model cards and evaluation tools are also useful for tracking model risks and transparency. These resources help developers and researchers connect the AI Act's systemic-risk requirements to practical testing and compliance workflows.
